title: Effects of light transitions on measures of alertness, arousal and comfort
research_question: How do subjective experiences and objective measures of vigilance, arousal and thermoregulation develop over time after an acute light transition?

participants.description: Thirty-eight healthy subjects (19 female; Mean age = 24, SD age = 2.9; range = 20-31 years old) from the Netherlands. Exclusion criteria: extreme chronotype (Midsleep < 3.8 or > 6.6), pregnancy, medication (other than contraceptive pill), hypertension or cardiovascular diseases, intercontinental travelling past three months. BMI Mean (SD) 22.0 (± 2.5), Range 18 to 30. PSQI score Mean (SD) 4.2 (± 1.5), Range 1.0 to 9.0. General Health (SF-36) Mean (SD) 73 (±13), Range 40 to 100.
participants.recruitment: Recruited via the J.F. Schouten School for User-System Interaction Research database and screened through an eligibility questionnaire.

stimuli_or_exposures.description: Two strongly contrasting light settings in a climate chamber (3.6 × 5.4 × 2.7m³). Warm, dim light (WD): CCT 2708 K, 97 lux on the eye. Cool, bright light (CB): CCT 5854 K, 1021 lux on the eye. Four conditions: Constant WD, WD to CB transition, Constant CB, CB to WD transition. Each session was 90 min, with a 45 min baseline (Phase I) and 45 min experimental phase (Phase II) with three 15-min measurement blocks.

mechanisms: Visual adaptation processes (IF pathway) for rapid onset and dissipation of visual appraisals and comfort.
Non-image forming (NIF) pathway for slower, persistent effects on alertness, vitality, and physiological arousal (SCL, DPG).
Anchoring of response range or relative nature of perceptual system for antecedent setting effects on visual sensation.
Complex interplay of physiological and psychological processes driving effects of light transitions.
moderators: Antecedent light setting (Phase I light condition)
Time of day (examined as control, but not as moderator due to sample size limitations)
implementation_implications: Abrupt light transitions can be used to temporarily induce vitality, alertness, or calmness in office environments.
When designing dynamic lighting scenarios, consider both the target light setting and the antecedent light setting, as the direction of transition matters.
Subjective experiences are valuable and do not always translate into performance enhancements, but contribute to quality of life.
Optimal time interval between light transition and measurement should account for transient and persistent trajectories of different variables.

limitations: CCT and illuminance were manipulated simultaneously, preventing attribution of effects to either variable alone.
Time of day was controlled by scheduling sessions at the same time for each participant, but its moderating effect could not be tested due to sample size.
Abrupt transitions were used; gradual transitions might yield different results.
Study conducted in a laboratory setting for 90 min; results need validation in longer field experiments.
Generalizability limited by participants from a specific cultural background.

stimulus_description.duration_exposure: Each light condition typically for 30-60 minutes, with transitions occurring between these periods.

theory_commitments.theory_name: Non-visual effects of light on human physiology and behavior
theory_commitments.specific_claim: Light characteristics (intensity, color temperature) and their transitions can acutely affect alertness, arousal, and comfort through non-visual pathways, independent of visual task performance.
Light exposure, particularly to short-wavelength light, can modulate circadian timing and melatonin suppression, thereby influencing sleepiness and alertness.

mechanism_chain.description: Light transitions activate intrinsically photosensitive retinal ganglion cells (ipRGCs), sending signals to the suprachiasmatic nucleus (SCN) and other brain regions, which in turn modulate physiological responses (e.g., heart rate, skin conductance) and neurocognitive states (e.g., alertness, arousal, comfort perception).
